title: Michael Burry Warns of 1987-Style Crash as S&P 500 Hits Fresh Record
excerpt: The Big Short investor maintains bearish bets against semiconductor stocks and compares the AI-driven rally to the final months of the dot-com bubble, even as the market climbs to new highs.
body:
• Michael Burry warns of a possible 1987-style crash, saying the S&P 500 hitting new highs will draw in new money that could amplify a reversal.
  • He maintains short positions against semiconductor stocks through put options on the iShares Semiconductor ETF and individual names including Nvidia, Tesla, and Micron.
  • Burry argues AI stock valuations are inflated by improper accounting, with the Nasdaq 100 trading closer to 43 times earnings when stock-based compensation and depreciation are properly factored in.
  • Paul Tudor Jones, who correctly predicted the 1987 crash, agrees the market resembles 1999 but estimates the rally could continue for another one to two years.

Michael Burry, the investor who predicted the 2008 housing crash and was portrayed in The Big Short, warned this week that the stock market may be approaching a major top with the potential for a 1987-style decline — even as the S&P 500 posted its first closing high in 42 sessions.

The Warning

"I continue to believe it is possible we are near a major top, and possible a 1987-type fall, but the S&P 500 making new highs will likely bring new money into the market," Burry wrote on X, excerpting from his Substack newsletter where he publishes analysis to more than 200,000 subscribers.

On October 19, 1987 — known as Black Monday — the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 22.6% in a single session, its worst-ever one-day percentage drop. Burry has invoked the analogy to describe what he sees as a mechanical vulnerability: as markets rise on falling volatility, systematic strategies employed by hedge funds automatically increase leverage, creating positions that can reverse rapidly if conditions shift.

"Remember, the market going up on falling volatility forces vol-targeting funds to leverage up, and brings leverage from other momentum strategies into play," Burry wrote.

The AI Trade as a Single Bet

Burry's concerns center on what he describes as a market dominated by a single theme. In a May 8 Substack post, written after a long drive during which he heard nothing but AI discussion on the radio, he compared the current moment to the final months of the 1999-2000 dot-com bubble.

"Stocks are not up or down because of jobs or consumer sentiment. They are going straight up because they have been going straight up. On a two letter thesis that everyone thinks they understand."

— Michael Burry, Substack

He has backed the thesis with money. Scion Asset Management disclosed put options on one million Nvidia shares and five million Palantir shares in late 2025, positions valued at 87 million and 12 million respectively. He has since widened his bets to include Tesla, Caterpillar, Applied Materials, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF. In July, he shorted Micron at ,051.87 after the stock rallied 700% over the prior year.

The Accounting Argument

Beyond sentiment, Burry has questioned the fundamental case for AI stock valuations. He argues that many AI companies use accounting practices that distort reported profits, particularly around stock-based compensation and the depreciation schedules applied to AI infrastructure.

When these adjustments are properly accounted for, Burry contends the Nasdaq 100 is trading closer to 43 times earnings rather than the roughly 30 times multiple that Wall Street consensus suggests. "History tells us that even if the party goes on for another week, month, three months, or year, the resolution will be to much lower prices," he wrote.

The Counterpoint

Burry himself acknowledges the risk of being early. "I am now a meme for the number of times I have called a crash. I have become the boy who cried wolf," he wrote in May. Analysis of his public calls between 2017 and 2023 shows roughly 71% of his major warnings did not play out. In January 2023, he posted a single word — "Sell" — before the S&P 500 went on to rise 17%.

On the same day Burry posted his latest warning, Paul Tudor Jones — who correctly predicted the 1987 crash — told CNBC that the market does feel like 1999 but estimated the rally could run for another one to two years. Two experienced investors, the same historical comparison, completely different conclusions about timing.

What It Means

The S&P 500's ability to reach new highs despite bearish positioning by prominent investors reflects the strength of AI-driven momentum. But Burry's widening bets against semiconductor stocks suggest he views the risk as structural rather than speculative. Whether the market proves him right this time or adds another entry to his record of early calls, the concentration of global equities in a single technology theme remains the central tension.
nri_angle: Indian investors with significant exposure to US tech stocks and semiconductor ETFs through platforms like Vested and INDmoney face direct portfolio risk if Burry's thesis on overvalued AI plays proves correct.
